Q1. Which of the following statements about using approximations in physics is
correct?
A. We can model a gymnast as a perfect sphere when predicting the torque on
their elbow during a flip.
This is incorrect because elbow torque depends on limb geometry, so a spherical model discards
essential shape details.
B. We can reasonably treat a school bus as a point mass when estimating how
far it travels along a highway in 20 minutes.
For mile-scale motion, the bus’s size is negligible compared with the travel distance, so a point-
mass model is appropriate for position change.
C. We are not allowed to assume a vacuum in any problem, even when we ex-
plicitly want to neglect air drag.
This is incorrect because “assume vacuum/no air resistance” is a standard idealization used to
simplify motion models.
D. None of the above is correct.
This is incorrect because option B is a valid, commonly used approximation for large-scale
motion.

Q2. Which of the following equations is correct?
A. 1 ms = 1 s.
This is incorrect because a millisecond is much smaller than a second.
B. 1 ms = 0.01 s.
This is incorrect because 0.01 s corresponds to 10 ms, not 1 ms.
C. 1 ms = 0.001 s.
This is correct because the prefix “milli-” means 10−3
, so 1 ms equals 0.001 s.
D. 1000 ms = 0.001 s.
This is incorrect because 1000 ms equals 1 s, not 0.001 s.

Q7. A tennis ball is launched with speed u0 at an angle ϕ above the horizontal
(ignore air resistance). What is the speed of the ball when it is at the maximum
height?
A. u0.
This is incorrect because the vertical component changes due to gravity, so the total speed
generally decreases before the peak.
B. u0 cos ϕ.
This is correct because at the top the vertical velocity is zero while the horizontal component
remains u0 cos ϕ, so the speed equals that value.
C. u0 sin ϕ.
This is incorrect because u0 sin ϕ is the initial vertical component, which is not the speed at
maximum height.
D. 0.
This is incorrect because only the vertical component becomes zero at the top, not the horizontal
component.

Q9. If the magnitudes of both charges are doubled and their separation is cut in
half, what happens to the magnitude of the electrostatic force that each charge
exerts on the other?
A. It stays the same.
This is incorrect because changing both charge and distance alters q1q2/r2
substantially.
B. It decreases by a factor of 4.
This is incorrect because halving the separation increases the force (due to the 1/r2 dependence)
rather than decreasing it.
C. It increases by a factor of 4.
This is incorrect because it accounts for doubling charges (factor 4) but ignores that halving
distance adds another factor of 4.
D. It increases by a factor of 16.
This is correct because F ∝ q1q2/r2
, so doubling both charges gives ×4 and halving distance
gives another ×4, for a total of ×16.
E. It increases by a factor of 8.
This is incorrect because the correct scaling combines to 4 × 4 = 16, not 8.

Q11. The force F⃗ = (−2.50 N)ˆı + (6.00 N)ˆȷ acts on a particle as it moves along
the y axis from y = −1.2 m to y = 3.8 m. What is the work, in joules, done by
the force on the particle?

of the dot product component along the motion.

x-displacement.
D. 0 J.
This is incorrect because the force has a nonzero component along the direction of motion (ˆȷ),
so the dot product is not zero.

Q12. A 3.0 kg sled initially moving at 4.0 m/s collides with a barrier and rebounds
at a speed of 1.5 m/s moving backward. The collision lasts for 0.15 seconds.
What is the average force exerted on the sled during the collision?
A. 110 N.
This is correct because ∆p = m(vf−vi) = 3.0(−1.5−4.0) = −16.5 kg m/s, so |Favg| = |∆p|/∆t =
16.5/0.15 = 110 N.
B. 73 N.
This is incorrect because it typically results from using the wrong time interval or an incorrect
velocity change.
C. 27.5 N.
This is incorrect because it corresponds to dividing the momentum change by 0.60 s (a common
arithmetic/time misread).
D. None of the above is correct.
This is incorrect because option A matches the impulse-momentum calculation.

Q13. A 65 kg astronaut is initially at rest in space. A 0.25 kg tool is moving
toward the astronaut at 18 m/s, and the astronaut catches it, holding on so they
move together afterward. What is the astronaut’s speed after catching the tool?
A. 0.069 m/s.
This is correct because conservation of momentum for a perfectly inelastic catch gives vf =
(0.25)(18)
65+0.25 ≈ 0.069 m/s.
B. 0.32 m/s.
This is incorrect because it comes from dividing by the astronaut’s mass incorrectly or using
only part of the total mass in the denominator.
C. 18 m/s.
This is incorrect because it ignores that momentum is shared with the astronaut, greatly re-
ducing the final speed.
D. 1.1 m/s.
This is incorrect because it overestimates the result by not accounting for the astronaut’s much
larger mass compared with the tool.
